Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by 

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & 1 \\ 6 & -4 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce $M$ to row echelon form.
questions.worked_solution:
Reducing $M$ to echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & 1 \\ 6 & -4 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3} \\ 6 & -4 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-6{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3} \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by 

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -3 \\ -7 & 14 & 21\end{aligned}].
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce $M$ to row echelon form, and then find the general solution of the linear system represented by the matrix.
questions.worked_solution:
Reducing $M$ to echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -3 \\ -7 & 14 & 21\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+7{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now

$$
{\begin{aligned}x-2y=-3 \\ 0x+0y=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since any pair of numbers $x,y$ is a solution of the final equation $0x+0y=0,$ we can remove this equation from the system. So, our system now consists of a single equation

$$
x-2y=-3.
$$

The first variable $(x)$ is the basic variable, and the second variable $(y)$ is the free variable. Solving for the basic variable $(x)$ in terms of the free variable $(y),$ we get $x=-3+2y,$ and the general solution is

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-3+2y \\ y=y\end{aligned}
$$

where $y$ is an arbitrary number. 

In vector form, the general solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3+2y \\ y\end{aligned}],\,y\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by 

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 3 \\ -3 & 3 & -9\end{aligned}].

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce $M$ to row echelon form, and then find the general solution of the linear system represented by the matrix.
questions.worked_solution:
Reducing $M$ to echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 3 \\ -3 & 3 & -9\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now

$$
{\begin{aligned}x-y=3 \\ 0x+0y=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since any pair of numbers $x,y$ is a solution of the final equation $0x+0y=0,$ we can remove this equation from the system. So, our system now consists of a single equation

$$
x-y=3.
$$

The first variable $(x)$ is the basic variable, and the second variable $(y)$ is the free variable. Solving for the basic variable $(x)$ in terms of the free variable $(y),$ we get $x=3+y,$ and the general solution is

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=3+y \\ y=y\end{aligned}
$$

where $y$ is an arbitrary number. 

In vector form, the general solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3+y \\ y\end{aligned}],\,y\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}x-6y=2 \\ -4x+24y=-10.\end{aligned}
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then find the general solution of the linear system.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we set up the augmented matrix for the system:

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & -6 & 2 \\ -4 & 24 & -10\end{aligned}]
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -6 & 2 \\ -4 & 24 & -10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -6 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now

$$
{\begin{aligned}x-6y=2 \\ 0x+0y=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

However, the final equation $0x+0y=-2$ has no solution. It simplifies to $0=-2,$ which is a false statement.

So, there is no pair $x,y$ that satisfies both equations in the system. Consequently, the overall system has no solution.

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Solving a Singular 2x2 System of Equations Using Gaussian Elimination
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the system of linear equations
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14118773/assets/bcbd79c8cac28ef6bb4dc07a04789692d9726df238b4907841825244432c5783.svg)
Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then find the general solution of the linear system.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we set up the augmented matrix for the system:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14118773/assets/d381e04f0a7eb2973e20c9f397ef2e2267f90ac6992cfacd3a8927b4d48138a9.svg)

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 5 & 4 \\ 4 & 10 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & \frac{5}{2} & 2 \\ 4 & 10 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-4){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & \frac{5}{2} & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & -8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14118773/assets/89ca081f99d8cbd33bb11e58ef6aa91aa3045a02ff06c9877a53b9e2f88874db.svg)

However, the final equation $0x+0y=-8$ has no solution. It simplifies to $0=-8,$ which is a false statement.

So, there is no pair $x,y$ that satisfies both equations in the system. Consequently, the overall system has no solution.

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Solving a Singular 2x2 System of Equations Using Gaussian Elimination

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Let's consider a system of linear equations where the corresponding coefficient matrix is singular. For example, consider the following system and its associated augmented matrix:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14118773/assets/6a69daf7712312876b0ec97c540bbc472e46a7938beb8a59e694a04ad0b1d8c6.svg)

To solve the system, we can reduce $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as usual. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -5 \\ -3 & 6 & 15\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14118773/assets/a8bfe3f6b27247ee9b27db8346fd94fb9068c85dec6f4a71517a821dee48dbf3.svg)

Since any pair of numbers $x,y$ is a solution of the final equation $0x+0y = 0,$ we can remove this equation from the system. So, our system now consists of a single equation

$$
x - 2y = -5.
$$

Finally, we describe the **general solution** of our system.

- The first variable in our equation, $x,$ is called a **basic variable**.

- The second variable in our equation, $y,$ is called a **free variable**.

Solving for the basic variable $(x)$ in terms of the free variable $(y),$ we get $x = -5+2y.$ So the general solution of the system is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14118773/assets/0ba4a232f29dd6fce2a8f6d7cda39b4f5b192c20fc91fe4403dfe648231382c5.svg)
where the free variable $y$ is any number.

In vector form, this solution is written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-5+2y \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+y[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,y\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this is the equation of a straight line on a plane. Any point on this line satisfies our system of equations.

If we want to find some **particular solution** of the system, we simply choose some particular value of $y$ and find the corresponding value of $x$ on the line. For example, if we choose $y=0,$ then the corresponding value is $x=-5$ and the particular solution is $x=-5,$ $y=0.$

tutorials.name: Singular Systems with No Solution
tutorials.problem:
Sometimes, a system of equations might not have any solutions. For example, consider the following augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}M=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 10\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14118773/assets/e8c64d8be247afd3e8ab02abc69e33635ef0234dbcbbc60f42379021a39a58a2.svg)

The final equation, $0x+0y=10,$ has no solution. It simplifies to $0=10,$ which is a false statement.

So, there is no pair $x,y$ that satisfies both equations in the system. Consequently, the overall system has no solution.

tutorials.name: The Number of Solutions of a 2x2 System
tutorials.problem:
Given a $2 \times 2$ system of linear equations, we have the following possibilities for the number of solutions:

- The system has exactly *one solution* if and only if the respective coefficient matrix is non-singular (meaning that the determinant is not zero). Such systems are called **consistent independent**.

- The system has *infinitely many solutions* if the second row in the standard echelon form contains only $0$'s. These systems are called **consistent dependent**.

- The system has *no solution* if the second row in the standard echelon form contains only $0$'s on the left-hand side and a non-zero element on the right-hand side. These are called **inconsistent** systems.

tutorials.title: The Number of Solutions of a 2x2 System
tutorials.content:
Given a $2 \times 2$ system of linear equations, we have the following possibilities for the number of solutions:

- The system has exactly *one solution* if and only if the respective coefficient matrix is non-singular (meaning that the determinant is not zero). Such systems are called **consistent independent**.

- The system has *infinitely many solutions* if the second row in the standard echelon form contains only $0$'s. These systems are called **consistent dependent**.

- The system has *no solution* if the second row in the standard echelon form contains only $0$'s on the left-hand side and a non-zero element on the right-hand side. These are called **inconsistent** systems.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14118773/assets/1692fbea298339ff839cf2f14986d51af45d1ec72b2b7d0de179336bdef40c0e.png)

where we have only $0$'s on the right-hand side, is called **homogeneous**. A homogeneous system always has at least one solution, namely, the solution $x=0$ and $y=0.$ Or, in vector form, $\langle 0,0 \rangle.$
